    global s
    assert s.count(a) == 1, a
    s = s.replace(a, b)

rep('''def test_prompt_version_is_v1():
    assert model.PROMPT_VERSION == "v1"
''', '''def test_prompt_version_is_v2():
    assert model.PROMPT_VERSION == "v2"
''')
rep('''    "a photo of one item, quantity in the body": ["photo", "nameplate", "picture"],
}
''', '''    "a photo of one item, quantity in the body": ["photo", "nameplate", "picture"],
    # v2
    "a vendor quote answers something we asked for": ["we asked", "our request", "our rfq"],
    "sales mail nobody asked for is not a vendor quote": ["unsolicited"],
    "raw is one line of the source, never several joined": ["never join", "do not join", "not several lines"],
    "on a tag or plate, raw is the line that identifies the item": ["identifies the item", "identifying line"],
}
''')
rep('''# ------------------------------------------------------------------ think first, then answer''', '''def dev_texts() -> dict[str, str]:
    """Everything a dev email says, as the model is shown it."""
    out = {}
    for path in sorted(DEV_EMAILS.glob("*.eml")):
        pk = reader.read_email(path)
        out[path.stem] = reader.render(pk, header=False)
    return out


def brief_text() -> str:
    """The public brief. Wording that is in the brief itself is not a dev leak."""
    return "\\n".join((ROOT / name).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
                     for name in ("ASSESSMENT.md", "data/README.md"))


def shingles(text: str, n: int) -> set[tuple[str, ...]]:
    words = norm(text).split()
    return {tuple(words[i:i + n]) for i in range(len(words) - n + 1)}


def test_prompt_shares_no_phrase_with_any_dev_email():
    """Stronger than checking answer-key lines: no run of five words from any dev email
    (body, quoted history, attachments) may appear in the prompt, unless the brief itself
    uses it. A rule learned from dev has to be restated as a rule, not quoted."""
    allowed = shingles(brief_text(), 5)
    prompt = shingles(PROMPT, 5) - allowed
    leaked = {eid: sorted(" ".join(s) for s in prompt & shingles(text, 5))
              for eid, text in dev_texts().items()}
    assert {eid: hits for eid, hits in leaked.items() if hits} == {}


def test_prompt_names_no_person_company_or_part_number_from_dev():
    """Names and identifiers are the purest dev strings: sender names, company names,
    and anything that looks like a model, RFQ or PO number (letters and digits mixed)."""
    brief = norm(brief_text())
    generic = {"sales", "purchasing", "supply", "pipe", "valve", "flange", "industrial", "team",
               "desk", "warehouse", "company", "service", "services", "group", "steel", "mill"}
    names, identifiers = set(), set()
    for path in sorted(DEV_EMAILS.glob("*.eml")):
        pk = reader.read_email(path)
        display, _, address = pk.sender.rpartition("<")
        domain = address.strip("> ").split("@")[-1]
        if domain == reader.INTERNAL_DOMAIN:
            continue
        for word in norm(display).split() + norm(domain.split(".")[0]).split():
            if len(word) >= 4 and word not in generic:
                names.add(word)
        for token in re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+(?:-[A-Za-z0-9]+)+|[A-Za-z]+\\d+[A-Za-z0-9]*", reader.render(pk)):
            if len(token) >= 6 and re.search(r"[A-Za-z]", token) and re.search(r"\\d{2,}", token):
                identifiers.add(token.lower())
    prompt_words = set(PROMPT_NORM.split())
    leaked_names = sorted(n for n in names if n in prompt_words and n not in brief.split())
    leaked_ids = sorted(i for i in identifiers if i in PROMPT.lower() and norm(i) not in brief)
    assert (leaked_names, leaked_ids) == ([], [])


def test_examples_in_the_prompt_are_not_dev_lines():
    """Every quoted example in the prompt must be absent from every dev email."""
    examples = [e for e in re.findall(r'"([^"\\n]{12,})"|\\'([^\\'\\n]{12,})\\'', PROMPT)]
    texts = {eid: norm(text) for eid, text in dev_texts().items()}
    brief = norm(brief_text())
    leaked = []
    for pair in examples:
        example = norm(pair[0] or pair[1])
        if len(example.split()) < 3 or example in brief:
            continue
        leaked += [f"{eid}: {example!r}" for eid, text in texts.items() if example in text]
    assert leaked == []


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ think first, then answer''')
p.write_text(s, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")
EOF

input.ask: Write prompt v2 against these tests?

content.text:
The prompt v2 tests are written in [tests/test_prompt.py](tests/test_prompt.py), and your reminder turned up a real problem: prompt v1 already quotes three phrases straight from dev emails. I've stopped before changing the prompt; 7 tests fail and 285 pass.

## The leak in prompt v1

I added stricter guards against fitting, and they caught these in the current prompt:

| Phrase in the prompt | Dev email it comes from |
|---|---|
| "line 2 is now 14" | E004 |
| "go ahead with items 1, 2 and 4" | E020 |
| "quote 3 of these" | E023 |

They came in through the "What the dev data taught us" section of CLAUDE.md, which quotes those emails, and I carried the wording into the prompt as examples. The original guard only compared the prompt against answer-key lines, sender domains and subjects, so it missed phrases from email bodies. The rules behind them are general, but the examples are dev strings, and v2 has to restate them with invented ones.

## The three new guards

- **No shared phrase:** no run of five words from any dev email (subject, body, quoted history, attachments) may appear in the prompt, unless the public brief itself uses it.
- **No names or identifiers:** no sender name, company name, or anything shaped like a model, RFQ or PO number from dev.
- **No dev examples:** every quoted example in the prompt must be absent from every dev email.

The first and third fail on v1; the second passes.

## The v2 rules the tests require

Each is stated as a property, satisfied by any of a few phrasings:

- A vendor quote answers something we asked for.
- Sales mail nobody asked for is not a vendor quote.
- `raw` is one line of the source, never several joined.
- On a tag or plate, `raw` is the line that identifies the item.

Plus the version bump to v2.

## What tests can't guarantee

These guards stop dev wording from entering the prompt. They can't stop a rule from being tuned to dev's answers, and the nameplate rule rests on a single dev example. The check for that is to try v2 on emails that aren't dev: a few invented ones we write ourselves (a promo from a made-up vendor, a tag photo, a resend), run through the real model for a few cents. I'd suggest building that small probe set right after v2.

The page-banding work is still uncommitted. Commit it first, then the tests:

```bash
git add rfqinbox/model.py cache parsed.json cost_report.json eval/history.md CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "Send large page images in full-resolution bands" -m "Dev quantity accuracy 94.3% to 100%; only the one scanned form was re-read."
```

```bash
git add tests/test_prompt.py && git commit -m "Add prompt v2 tests and stricter dev-leak guards (failing)" -m "Guards catch three dev phrases quoted in prompt v1."
```

Here's what's left, measured against the hand-in list in ASSESSMENT.md. The parser itself is nearly done; most of the remaining work is the write-ups and the recording. It's all due Sunday 15 November, 23:59 CST.

## Finish the parser (about 1–2 hours)

1. **Prompt v2.** The failing tests are committed. I write the prompt, you do one paid re-run of dev (about $0.27), and I score it. This fixes the three dev phrases quoted in v1, plus the promo and nameplate rules.
2. **A small probe set (recommended).** A few invented emails that aren't dev, run through the real model for a few cents. It's the only real check that we haven't fitted dev, and it gives you something concrete for the "predicted held-out numbers" section.
3. **Confirm the model and price.** `gpt-4.1` at $2.00 / $8.00 per million tokens is still from my memory; check it against OpenAI's pricing page.
4. **Fresh-clone check.** Clone into a new folder, run the one setup step, then `parse` on dev with no key. This is exactly what the graders do first.
5. **Pin dependency versions.** The no-key replay depends on the reader producing the same text on the graders' machine, and unpinned libraries are the main risk to that.

## Required documents (about 2–3 hours)

6. **RUNNING.md.** It exists but needs finishing: final cost per run, what the graders need on Windows, and the link to the recording.
7. **DECISIONS.md**, at most two pages, with the four required sections:
   - something in the data that surprised you;
   - something in the brief you disagree with, and what you did;
   - predicted held-out numbers and the two kinds of email you expect to get wrong;
   - how this runs for real (3,000 emails a day, provider down for two hours, a 300-page PDF, the same email delivered twice), and which of those you actually built.
   
   It also needs roughly how long you spent.
8. **AI_USAGE.md**, at most one page: setup, how you worked, and three moments, each with a commit hash and the session it happened in.
9. **`ai-sessions/`.** Copy this project's session logs from `~/.claude/projects/`, search them for `sk-`, and redact anything found.
10. **Screen recording**, five minutes or less: one email end to end, two decisions you'd defend, and one moment where you changed the agent's course.

## Before sending

11. Regenerate `parsed.json` and `cost_report.json` one last time and run `check_format.py`.
12. Push. Your branch is ahead of `origin/main`.

## Known gaps to state in DECISIONS.md, not necessarily fix

- **Not tested on Windows.** The code is written for it, but it has only run on Linux here.
- **Two runs at once both pay.** There is no lock on the cache.
- **Model down means everything is flagged.** There is no rule-based fallback.
- **Duplicates need the same sender.** A customer resending from a different address is treated as a new request.

## Optional

- The catalog matcher (design in MATCHER.md, or built).
- The small web app.

Neither affects your score; I'd only start them if the required items are done with time to spare.

For the three moments in AI_USAGE.md, this session already has good candidates: the size-as-quantity rule I got wrong and the score caught, your reminder that led to finding dev phrases in the prompt, and the scan-shrinking diagnosis on E009.

Shall I write prompt v2 now?

Prompt v2 is written and all 292 tests pass, including the three new dev-leak guards. It hasn't been run against the model yet, so I can't tell you whether it scores better or worse than v1.

What changed in the prompt ([rfqinbox/model.py](rfqinbox/model.py)):
- **Vendor quote:** now defined as a supplier answering something we asked for. Unsolicited sales mail (a flyer, promo price list, stock list or newsletter) is `other`, even when it lists items and prices.
- **`raw`:** one line of the source, never several joined. On a tag, nameplate or label it is the single line that identifies the item; the rest goes in `description`.
- **Dev phrases removed:** the three examples quoted from dev emails are gone. The rules they illustrated are now stated without an example (a new quantity for one item, an item cancelled, an item added; a go-ahead on some lines of our quote; the body saying how many are wanted).

I also added a line to CLAUDE.md saying prompt examples must be invented, because its "What the dev data taught us" section quotes dev emails and that is how the phrases got into v1.

Commit the prompt first, so the new cache lands as its own commit:

```bash
git add rfqinbox/model.py CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "Add prompt v2" -m "Vendor quote must answer our request; raw is one source line; no wording taken from dev."
```

Then re-run dev. This pays for all 24 emails, about $0.30:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m rfqinbox parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
```

Run it once and let it finish; starting a second run while the first is going pays twice.

When it's done I'll score it against v1. If v2 comes out worse, reverting the prompt text restores the v1 results for free, since those answers are still in `cache/`.

"""Builds the probe inbox: invented emails that are NOT the dev set.

    python eval/make_probes.py        ->  eval/probes/emails/P*.eml + eval/probes/answer_key.json

Why: dev is what the prompt and the checks were built against, so a good dev score
says little about emails nobody has seen. Every probe here is made up - companies,
people, part numbers, wording - and reproduces a *kind* of surprise from the brief
(section headings, a hidden old revision, a resend, a revision, a forward, a tag
photo, a phone scan, a bounce ...). They were written once, before the system was
run on them, and are scored with the same scorer as dev:

    python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
    python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json

Limits, stated plainly: the author of these probes also wrote the prompt, so they
test whether the rules generalise to new strings, not whether the rules are the
right ones. A probe that fails is a finding; fix the general property, never the probe.

Needs the dev requirements (reportlab) as well as the runtime ones.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import io
import json
from email.message import EmailMessage
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "probes"
RFQ_DESK = "Ridgeline RFQ Desk <rfq@ridgeline-supply.example>"
XLSX = "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"

EMAILS: dict[str, EmailMessage] = {}
KEY: dict[str, dict] = {}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ builders

def email(pid, sender, subject, date, body, *, attachments=(), reply_to=None, to=RFQ_DESK):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"], msg["To"], msg["Subject"], msg["Date"] = sender, to, subject, date
    msg["Message-ID"] = f"<{pid.lower()}.{abs(hash(subject)) % 10**6:06d}@probe.example>" \
        if pid not in MESSAGE_IDS else MESSAGE_IDS[pid]
    if reply_to:
        msg["In-Reply-To"] = reply_to
        msg["References"] = reply_to
    msg.set_content(body)
    for name, mime, data in attachments:
        if mime == "message/rfc822":
            msg.add_attachment(data)
        else:
            maintype, subtype = mime.split("/", 1)
            msg.add_attachment(data, maintype=maintype, subtype=subtype, filename=name)
    EMAILS[pid] = msg
    return msg


MESSAGE_IDS = {"P01": "<20261103081200.a41c@tidewaterprocess.example>"}


def key(pid, classification, lines=(), *, revises=None, duplicate_of=None, needs_review=False):
    KEY[pid] = {
        "classification": classification, "revises": revises, "duplicate_of": duplicate_of,
        "needs_review": needs_review,
        "line_items": [dict(id=f"{pid}-{n}", **ln) for n, ln in enumerate(lines, 1)],
    }


def ln(raw, qty, uom="EA", source="body", must=(), must_not=(), qty_tol=0):
    return {"raw": raw, "qty": qty, "qty_tol": qty_tol, "uom": uom, "source": source,
            "must_mention": list(must), "must_not_mention": list(must_not)}


def font(size):
    return ImageFont.load_default(size=size)


def png(im) -> bytes:
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    im.save(buf, format="PNG")
    return buf.getvalue()

}

    python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json

test whether the rules generalise to new strings, not whether the rules are the

def email(pid, sender, subject, date, body, *, attachments=(), reply_to=None, to=RFQ_DESK):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"], msg["To"], msg["Subject"], msg["Date"] = sender, to, subject, date
    msg["Message-ID"] = f"<{pid.lower()}.{abs(hash(subject)) % 10**6:06d}@probe.example>" \
        if pid not in MESSAGE_IDS else MESSAGE_IDS[pid]
    if reply_to:
        msg["In-Reply-To"] = reply_to
        msg["References"] = reply_to
    msg.set_content(body)
    for name, mime, data in attachments:
        if mime == "message/rfc822":
            msg.add_attachment(data)
        else:
            maintype, subtype = mime.split("/", 1)
            msg.add_attachment(data, maintype=maintype, subtype=subtype, filename=name)
    EMAILS[pid] = msg
    return msg

"""Builds the probe inbox: invented emails that are NOT the dev set.

    python eval/make_probes.py        ->  eval/probes/emails/P*.eml + eval/probes/answer_key.json

Why: dev is what the prompt and the checks were built against, so a good dev score
says little about emails nobody has seen. Every probe here is made up - companies,
people, part numbers, wording - and reproduces a *kind* of surprise from the brief
(section headings, a hidden old revision, a resend, a revision, a forward, a tag
photo, a phone scan, a bounce ...). They were written once, before the system was
run on them, and are scored with the same scorer as dev:

    python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
    python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json

Limits, stated plainly: the author of these probes also wrote the prompt, so they
test whether the rules generalise to new strings, not whether the rules are the
right ones. A probe that fails is a finding; fix the general property, never the probe.

Needs the dev requirements (reportlab) as well as the runtime ones.
"""

def email(pid, sender, subject, date, body, *, attachments=(), reply_to=None, to=RFQ_DESK):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"], msg["To"], msg["Subject"], msg["Date"] = sender, to, subject, date
    msg["Message-ID"] = f"<{pid.lower()}.{abs(hash(subject)) % 10**6:06d}@probe.example>" \
        if pid not in MESSAGE_IDS else MESSAGE_IDS[pid]
    if reply_to:
        msg["In-Reply-To"] = reply_to
        msg["References"] = reply_to
    msg.set_content(body)
    for name, mime, data in attachments:
        if mime == "message/rfc822":
            msg.add_attachment(data)
        else:
            maintype, subtype = mime.split("/", 1)
            msg.add_attachment(data, maintype=maintype, subtype=subtype, filename=name)
    EMAILS[pid] = msg
    return msg

"""Builds the probe inbox: invented emails that are NOT the dev set.

    python eval/make_probes.py        ->  eval/probes/emails/P*.eml + eval/probes/answer_key.json

Why: dev is what the prompt and the checks were built against, so a good dev score
says little about emails nobody has seen. Every probe here is made up - companies,
people, part numbers, wording - and reproduces a *kind* of surprise from the brief
(section headings, a hidden old revision, a resend, a revision, a forward, a tag
photo, a phone scan, a bounce ...). They were written once, before the system was
run on them, and are scored with the same scorer as dev:

    python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
    python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json

Limits, stated plainly: the author of these probes also wrote the prompt, so they
test whether the rules generalise to new strings, not whether the rules are the
right ones. A probe that fails is a finding; fix the general property, never the probe.

Needs the dev requirements (reportlab) as well as the runtime ones.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import io
import json
from email.message import EmailMessage
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "probes"
RFQ_DESK = "Ridgeline RFQ Desk <rfq@ridgeline-supply.example>"
XLSX = "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet"

EMAILS: dict[str, EmailMessage] = {}
KEY: dict[str, dict] = {}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ builders

def email(pid, sender, subject, date, body, *, attachments=(), reply_to=None, to=RFQ_DESK):
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"], msg["To"], msg["Subject"], msg["Date"] = sender, to, subject, date
    msg["Message-ID"] = f"<{pid.lower()}.{abs(hash(subject)) % 10**6:06d}@probe.example>" \
        if pid not in MESSAGE_IDS else MESSAGE_IDS[pid]
    if reply_to:
        msg["In-Reply-To"] = reply_to
        msg["References"] = reply_to
    msg.set_content(body)
    for name, mime, data in attachments:
        if mime == "message/rfc822":
            msg.add_attachment(data)
        else:
            maintype, subtype = mime.split("/", 1)
            msg.add_attachment(data, maintype=maintype, subtype=subtype, filename=name)
    EMAILS[pid] = msg
    return msg


MESSAGE_IDS = {"P01": "<20261103081200.a41c@tidewaterprocess.example>"}


def key(pid, classification, lines=(), *, revises=None, duplicate_of=None, needs_review=False):
    KEY[pid] = {
        "classification": classification, "revises": revises, "duplicate_of": duplicate_of,
        "needs_review": needs_review,
        "line_items": [dict(id=f"{pid}-{n}", **ln) for n, ln in enumerate(lines, 1)],
    }


def ln(raw, qty, uom="EA", source="body", must=(), must_not=(), qty_tol=0):
    return {"raw": raw, "qty": qty, "qty_tol": qty_tol, "uom": uom, "source": source,
            "must_mention": list(must), "must_not_mention": list(must_not)}


def font(size):
    return ImageFont.load_default(size=size)


def png(im) -> bytes:
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    im.save(buf, format="PNG")
    return buf.getvalue()

def bom_workbook() -> bytes:
    import openpyxl
    from openpyxl.styles import Font

    wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
    ws = wb.active
    ws.title = "BOM Rev 2"
    ws.append(["ALL FITTINGS BLACK MALLEABLE IRON 150# THREADED"])
    ws.merge_cells("A1:D1")
    ws.append(["ITEM", "QTY", "UOM", "DESCRIPTION"])
    ws.append([1, 24, "EA", '1" 90 elbow'])
    ws.append([2, 12, "EA", '1" tee'])

    for cell in ws[5]:
        cell.font = Font(strike=True)
    ws.append([4, 10, "EA", '1-1/4" x 1" reducing coupling'])
    ws.append([5, 40, "FT", '1" pipe SCH 40 A53B T&C'])

    old.append([2, 18, "EA", '3/4" tee'])
    old.append([3, 60, "FT", '3/4" pipe SCH 40'])

MI = ("malleable|mi", "150", "threaded|npt|thd")

      "Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:30:00 -0600", "Hi,\n\nBill of material attached for pricing.\n\nThanks\nOmar\n",
      attachments=[(BOM_NAME, XLSX, BOM)])

    ln('1 | 24 | EA | 1" 90 elbow', 24, source=BOM_NAME, must=MI),
    ln('2 | 12 | EA | 1" tee', 12, source=BOM_NAME, must=MI),
    ln('4 | 10 | EA | 1-1/4" x 1" reducing coupling', 10, source=BOM_NAME, must=MI),
    ln('5 | 40 | FT | 1" pipe SCH 40 A53B T&C', 40, "FT", source=BOM_NAME,

The probe set is built: 17 invented emails with a 39-line answer key, in the same format as dev so the same scorer works. The reader handles all of them, but none has been through the model yet, so there are no results.

Everything in them is made up: companies, people, part numbers and wording. Each reproduces a kind of surprise from the brief:

| Probe | What it tests |
|---|---|
| P01 | Section headings, an "unless noted" default, a line that overrides it, a spelled-out quantity |
| P02 | Unsolicited promo price list (should be `other`) |
| P03 | A supplier answering our request (`vendor_quote`) |
| P04, P05 | Status inquiry; out-of-office reply |
| P06 | Spreadsheet with a merged header, a struck-through row, a totals row and a hidden old revision |
| P07 | The same request resent the next day with different wording (duplicate of P06) |
| P08 | A revision of P01: one quantity changed, one item cancelled, one added |
| P09 | A PO accepting two of three lines on our quoted quote |
| P10 | Our own rep forwarding a customer, with a note that changes a quantity |
| P11 | "Attached" but only a logo came |
| P12 | A tag photo with the quantity in the body |
| P13 | A phone scan of a form with small text and section rows (exercises page banding) |
| P14 | Items identified only by a past order |
| P15 | A bounce carrying our own outgoing RFQ |
| P16 | Spelled-out, vague and size-heavy quantities |
| P17 | A password-protected PDF |

The files are [eval/make_probes.py](eval/make_probes.py) (the generator, which documents how each was made) and `eval/probes/` (the emails and `answer_key.json`).

Two caveats:
- **I wrote both the probes and the prompt.** They test whether the rules carry over to new strings, not whether the rules are the right ones.
- **P12 is the same kind as dev's one remaining miss.** If the tag's `raw` comes back joined again, that confirms it's a general weakness and not a dev quirk.

Run them with their own cache so they don't mix with dev's. This pays for 17 emails, roughly $0.15–0.20:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
```

I haven't looked at any model output for these, and I won't change the key after seeing results unless the key itself is wrong, in which case I'll tell you what and why. Once it's run I'll score it, and then propose one commit for the probes together with their results.

content.text:
The probes scored well on their first run, with no changes to anything after seeing the output: no silent losses, every email classified correctly, and 38 of 39 lines found. The run cost $0.12.

| Measure | Probes (17 emails) |
|---|---|
| Silent losses | 0 |
| Hallucinated lines | 1 |
| Lost / phantom requests | 0 / 0 |
| Classification | 100% |
| Line recall and precision | 38/39 |
| Quantity, unit, source | 100% each |
| Context carried | 94.7% |
| Links (duplicate, revises) | 100% |
| Needs-review precision / recall | 100% / 100% |

What held up on unseen strings:
- **The harder cases all worked:** the resend was caught as a duplicate, the revision rebuilt the complete order and linked to its original, the partial PO took the right two lines, and the rep's note changed the forwarded quantity.
- **Nothing leaked through:** the hidden sheet, struck row and totals row produced no lines; the promo, the vendor reply and the bounce carrying our own RFQ were not treated as requests.
- **The scanned form read correctly:** all eleven rows, every quantity right, through the page banding.

## Two real weaknesses

**The tag photo's `raw` is joined again (P12).** It's the same failure as dev's E023: the model returned every line of the tag as one `raw`, so it doesn't pair with the key. The item, quantity and source are correct. Two out of two of this kind fail, so it's a general weakness, not a dev quirk.

**A partial override drops the rest of the default (P01 and P08).** The email says all pipe is SCH 80 A106B seamless unless noted, and one line says SCH 40. The model's description kept SCH 40 but dropped A106B seamless. My prompt wording caused this: it says a default "must not appear" on a line that overrides it, which the model read as dropping the whole default, not just the schedule. Dev never showed it because no dev line overrides only part of a default.

## Suggested fixes

- **Tag `raw`: fix in code.** The prompt rule already exists and the model ignores it. For a line read from a picture whose `raw` is several lines or several labelled fields, code keeps the one that carries the model or part number. Which line the graders want is a guess based on one dev example.
- **Partial override: fix in the prompt.** State that an override replaces only the attribute it restates, and the rest of the default still applies. That means prompt v3 and a paid re-run of both sets, about $0.40.

I've added a "Probe inbox" section to [eval/history.md](eval/history.md) with this baseline and the two findings. I'd commit the probes now, before any fix, so the history shows they were written first:

```bash
git add eval/make_probes.py eval/probes eval/history.md && git commit -m "Add probe inbox: 17 invented emails with a key" -m "First run: 0 silent losses, 38/39 lines; found joined tag raw and partial-override context loss."
```

The failing tests for both probe findings are written, and I've stopped before the code. 8 fail as expected and 299 pass.

## Prompt v3 ([tests/test_prompt.py](tests/test_prompt.py))

- The version must be `v3`.
- The prompt must state that an override replaces only what it restates, and the rest of the default still applies.
- **The leak guards now cover the probe emails too.** The probes are measurement data like dev, so quoting them in the prompt would fit them. The current prompt passes these guards.

## One-line `raw` for tags ([tests/test_checks.py](tests/test_checks.py))

For a line read from a picture, when `raw` is several lines or several labelled fields, code keeps only the part that carries a model, part, catalog or figure number. The description, quantity and source are untouched. All test tags are invented.

Six cases must be cut down: lines separated by newlines, labelled fields on one line, and part, catalog and figure numbers in different spellings.

Eight cases must be left exactly as the model read them:
- a tag with no identifying line;
- a label with no number after it;
- a serial number only, since that identifies one unit and not the item;
- ordinary single lines from a handwritten list or scanned form, including ones that happen to mention a model;
- any line from text the reader extracted, which is never rewritten.

## Judgment calls

- **Which line to keep is a guess.** The README says `raw` is one line as it appears. That the graders want the model-number line comes from one dev example, and my probe key follows the same convention because I wrote it.
- **When there's no identifying line, code does nothing.** It doesn't pick a line at random.

Prompt v3 fixed the partial-override problem on the probes, and after one more change to the tag rule the probes score 39 of 39 lines with nothing hallucinated. Dev isn't scored yet: only 8 of its 24 emails have v3 answers in the cache.

| Measure | Probes, v2 | Probes, v3 + tag rule |
|---|---|---|
| Silent losses | 0 | 0 |
| Hallucinated lines | 1 | 0 |
| Classification | 100% | 100% |
| Line recall and precision | 38/39 | 39/39 |
| Quantity | 100% | 100% |
| Unit | 100% | 97.4% |
| Context carried | 94.7% | 100% |
| Links, needs-review | 100% | 100% |

## Things you should know

- **I widened the tag rule after seeing a probe result.** Under v3 the model returned the tag as one run of text with no line breaks and no colons, a third format my rule didn't cover. I added two failing test cases with invented tags, then widened the rule: three or more nameplate field names (model, size, body, class and so on) in text that doesn't start with a count is treated as a tag read out in full. This is the one place the probes influenced the code, and it relies on a list of field names, so a tag with unusual wording could still slip through.
- **The one unit error is my key, not the system.** For `6" DI pipe, class 350 - enough to run about 60 ft`, my key says no unit and the model returned `FT` with a blank quantity. The customer did write "ft", so the model's answer is at least as defensible. I've left the key as I wrote it and not changed it to match the output.
- **Dev looks mid-run or interrupted.** If it's still going, let it finish. If it was stopped, run it again; it only pays for the 16 emails it's missing:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m rfqinbox parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
```

All 310 tests pass. I'll propose the commits once dev is scored, so the tag-rule change, both result sets and the history rows go in together.

# Running

Requires **Python 3.11+**. No Docker, no shell-outs, no system packages: every dependency
ships prebuilt wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux. Developed on Linux; written for native
Windows (pathlib, explicit UTF-8, LF output) but **not yet run on Windows** — see DECISIONS.md.

## Setup (one step)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Run

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

- Reads every `.eml` in `<dir>`, writes `parsed.json`, and writes `cost_report.json` next to it.
- Reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment. For local runs a `.env` file in the current
  folder is also loaded (`OPENAI_API_KEY=...`); a variable already set in the environment wins.
  `.env` is git-ignored.
- With **no key** it replays recorded answers from `cache/` and flags any email it has no
  answer for (`rfq` + `needs_review`). It never crashes on a missing key or a failed call.
- A second run on the same inbox makes **no model calls**: answers are cached under a hash of
  everything the model was shown. New answers (for example the held-out inbox) are written to
  `cache/`; `--cache <dir>` or `RFQINBOX_CACHE_DIR` moves it.

Dev, exactly as committed (no key needed):

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
python data/check_format.py parsed.json --emails data/dev/emails
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json
```

## Model and cost

- **Model:** OpenAI `gpt-4.1`, Chat Completions, strict JSON-schema output, images sent inline.
  One call per email (a second only if the reply is malformed). Override with `RFQINBOX_MODEL`.
- **Dev run:** 24 emails, 24 calls, 66,139 input / 19,913 output tokens, **$0.29**
  (about 1.2 cents per email; median 0.9 cents; the dearest are a 44-line PDF and a two-page
  phone scan at about 3.5 cents each). About 2 minutes, sequential.
- **Per email:** `cost_report.json` lists calls, tokens and dollars for every email;
  `calls`/`cost_usd` are what the answer cost when it was made, `new_calls`/`new_cost_usd` are
  what this run spent (zero on a replay). The totals are printed on stderr.
- **Expect** roughly $0.50 and 3–4 minutes for a 40-email inbox.
- Prices are a table in `rfqinbox/model.py` ($2.00 / $8.00 per million input / output tokens).

## Other commands

```
python -m rfqinbox inspect data/dev/emails/E005.eml     # what the model is shown for one email
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json --gate             # exit 1 on any silent loss
```

## Tests (no key, no network)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest
```

The tests remove `OPENAI_API_KEY` and switch `.env` loading off, so they can never spend money.

## The probe inbox

`eval/probes/` holds 17 invented emails (not dev) with their own key and cache; see
`eval/make_probes.py` and `eval/history.md`.

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json
```

# Decisions

Time spent: TODO (hours). One model call per email; everything checkable without judgment is code.

## Something in the data that surprised me

The biggest source of wrong output was an email the model read perfectly. A customer resent
an RFQ a day later with different wording and the same PDF. The model extracted all 44 lines
correctly, and every one of them was wrong, because the README says the later copy has no
lines. 44 of the first run's 45 hallucinated lines were that one email. Whether an answer is
right depended on a different email, so no prompt could fix it. That moved duplicates and
revision links out of the model entirely (`checks.link_records`).

## Something in the brief I disagree with, and what I did

`needs_review` is allowed only on requests. That leaves no honest answer for "I could not read
this and do not know what it is": calling it `other` risks a silent loss, the most expensive
failure. So anything unreadable or failed becomes `rfq` + `needs_review`. I accept the cost: if
the model is down, a vendor quote is reported as a request needing review (a phantom) rather
than dropped. I would rather the contract had an `unknown` class or allowed the flag everywhere.

Second, smaller: `raw` for a picture is "your reading of it", but lines are paired on `raw`
tokens. A nameplate has no single line, and the dev key uses only the model-number line. I
followed that (a code rule keeps the identifying line), but it is a guess from one example.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 210/210 lines and my own 17-email probe set is 39/39, but dev shaped the rules and I
wrote the probes, so I discount both.

| | prediction (~40 emails) |
|---|---|
| silent losses | 0 |
| hallucinated lines | 0–8 (one missed duplicate would be most of it) |
| lost / phantom requests | 0–1 / 0–1 |
| classification | 93–97% |
| line recall / precision | 94–98% / 93–98% |
| qty / uom / source | 96–99% / 97–100% / 97–100% |
| context carried | 90–96% |
| revises / duplicate links | 70–100% (few emails, so coarse) |
| needs_review precision / recall | 75–100% / 80–100% |

1. **Dense phone scans and photos.** The same scanned form gave 12 wrong quantities, then 0,
   then 1 across three runs. Sending pages in full-resolution bands fixed most of it, but
   small digits are still occasionally misread, and code cannot check a number that exists
   only in a picture.
2. **Threads and resends that do not look like dev's.** Duplicates need the same sender and
   either identical lines or provably identical content; a resend from a colleague's address,
   or a re-typed list, stays a normal request and all its lines count as hallucinated. A
   revision whose original is not quoted is rebuilt from whatever is in the email.

## How this runs for real

- **3,000 emails a day by webhook.** Each email is independent until linking, about 5 s and
  1.2 cents (roughly $36/day). *Built:* per-email isolation, atomic writes, a content-keyed
  cache, cost per email. *Not built:* the queue and workers; linking duplicates and revisions
  against a rolling window of earlier mail instead of one folder.
- **Provider down for two hours.** *Built:* timeouts, three retries with backoff on 429/5xx
  and network errors, then the email is flagged with the reason; failures are never cached,
  so the next run retries only those. *Not built:* a retry queue. In production I would park
  the email and alert, not emit a flagged record after 15 seconds.
- **A 300-page PDF.** *Built:* the reader stops at 40 text pages, 6 scanned pages and 60,000
  characters, says so in the text the model sees, and code flags the email for review with
  the lines it did read. *Not built:* splitting a long document across several calls.
- **The same email delivered twice.** *Built:* the second copy costs nothing (same cache key)
  and is marked `duplicate_of` the first. *Not built:* a lock. Two runs started at once both
  pay; I did this by accident and it cost $0.16.

## Where the model decides and where code decides

The model decides what kind of email it is, which text is a request, and what applies to each
line (headings, defaults and overrides, form fields, the rep's note on a forward). It writes
an `analysis` field first, kept in the cache and never in `parsed.json`.

Code decides everything that needs no judgment: what is quoted history, hidden or struck
through (the reader marks it before the model sees it); the output schema (one repair retry);
that every line's words appear in the email, else it is dropped and the email flagged; that
lines found only in hidden or struck content are dropped; `source` names; vague amounts and
sizes are not quantities; missing, unreadable, encrypted or truncated attachments are
flagged; duplicates and `revises`; and that a request with no lines is never left unflagged.

## How I measured

`rfqinbox score` implements the README's grading as I read it (the pairing threshold is my
guess); `eval/history.md` has a row per behaviour change. Dev alone could not tell me whether
I had fitted it, so I wrote `eval/probes/`: 17 invented emails. Their first run found two
real faults dev never showed (a partial override dropping the rest of a default; a nameplate
`raw`). Tests fail if the prompt contains any five-word run, name or part number from a dev
or probe email. That guard caught three dev phrases I had used as examples in prompt v1.

## Rejected, broken, next

- **Rejected:** the OpenAI SDK (one POST does not need it); local OCR (no wheels-only
  option); separate classify and extract calls (double the cost, no gain on dev); a
  rule-based classifier for when the model is down (a wrong confident answer is worse than
  a flag); fuzzy duplicate thresholds (a real one-line change would vanish).
- **Known broken or unverified:** not run on Windows; replay with no key depends on the
  reader producing the same text with the graders' library versions (unpinned); the tag rule
  relies on a list of field names; the price table is not checked against the live price list.
- **Next:** read scans twice and flag disagreements; pin versions; a queue; the matcher.

   either identical lines or provably identical content; a resend from a colleague's address,
   or a re-typed list, stays a normal request and all its lines count as hallucinated. A
   revision whose original is not quoted is rebuilt from whatever is in the email.

## How this runs for real

diff, and the agent's list of judgment calls, and I pushed back on those: three of them were

number from any dev email), which failed on v1, and v2 (`874c5ed`) removed the phrases.

gave me shell commands to load `.env`; they did not work from the app's command box and cost
several failed runs. I told it to load `.env` in code. It did (`e1bb609`), and added what I
had not asked for but needed: the real environment wins, and tests switch loading off so

# Running

Requires **Python 3.11+**. No Docker, no shell-outs, no system packages: every dependency
ships prebuilt wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux. Developed on Linux; written for native
Windows (pathlib, explicit UTF-8, LF output) but **not yet run on Windows** — see DECISIONS.md.

## Setup (one step)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Run

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

- Reads every `.eml` in `<dir>`, writes `parsed.json`, and writes `cost_report.json` next to it.
- Reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment. For local runs a `.env` file in the current
  folder is also loaded (`OPENAI_API_KEY=...`); a variable already set in the environment wins.
  `.env` is git-ignored.
- With **no key** it replays recorded answers from `cache/` and flags any email it has no
  answer for (`rfq` + `needs_review`). It never crashes on a missing key or a failed call.
- A second run on the same inbox makes **no model calls**: answers are cached under a hash of
  everything the model was shown. New answers (for example the held-out inbox) are written to
  `cache/`; `--cache <dir>` or `RFQINBOX_CACHE_DIR` moves it.

Dev, exactly as committed (no key needed):

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
python data/check_format.py parsed.json --emails data/dev/emails
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json
```

## Model and cost

- **Model:** OpenAI `gpt-4.1`, Chat Completions, strict JSON-schema output, images sent inline.
  One call per email (a second only if the reply is malformed). Override with `RFQINBOX_MODEL`.
- **Dev run:** 24 emails, 24 calls, 66,139 input / 19,913 output tokens, **$0.29**
  (about 1.2 cents per email; median 0.9 cents; the dearest are a 44-line PDF and a two-page
  phone scan at about 3.5 cents each). About 2 minutes, sequential.
- **Per email:** `cost_report.json` lists calls, tokens and dollars for every email;
  `calls`/`cost_usd` are what the answer cost when it was made, `new_calls`/`new_cost_usd` are
  what this run spent (zero on a replay). The totals are printed on stderr.
- **Expect** roughly $0.50 and 3–4 minutes for a 40-email inbox.
- Prices are a table in `rfqinbox/model.py` ($2.00 / $8.00 per million input / output tokens).

## Other commands

```
python -m rfqinbox inspect data/dev/emails/E005.eml     # what the model is shown for one email
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json --gate             # exit 1 on any silent loss
```

## Tests (no key, no network)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest
```

The tests remove `OPENAI_API_KEY` and switch `.env` loading off, so they can never spend money.

## The probe inbox

`eval/probes/` holds 17 invented emails (not dev) with their own key and cache; see
`eval/make_probes.py` and `eval/history.md`.

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json
```

# Running

Requires **Python 3.11+**. No Docker, no shell-outs, no system packages: every dependency
ships prebuilt wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux. Developed on Linux; written for native
Windows (pathlib, explicit UTF-8, LF output) but **not yet run on Windows** — see DECISIONS.md.

## Setup (one step)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Run

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails <dir> --out parsed.json
```

- Reads every `.eml` in `<dir>`, writes `parsed.json`, and writes `cost_report.json` next to it.
- Reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` from the environment. For local runs a `.env` file in the current
  folder is also loaded (`OPENAI_API_KEY=...`); a variable already set in the environment wins.
  `.env` is git-ignored.
- With **no key** it replays recorded answers from `cache/` and flags any email it has no
  answer for (`rfq` + `needs_review`). It never crashes on a missing key or a failed call.
- A second run on the same inbox makes **no model calls**: answers are cached under a hash of
  everything the model was shown. New answers (for example the held-out inbox) are written to
  `cache/`; `--cache <dir>` or `RFQINBOX_CACHE_DIR` moves it.

Dev, exactly as committed (no key needed):

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails data/dev/emails --out parsed.json
python data/check_format.py parsed.json --emails data/dev/emails
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json
```

## Model and cost

- **Model:** OpenAI `gpt-4.1`, Chat Completions, strict JSON-schema output, images sent inline.
  One call per email (a second only if the reply is malformed). Override with `RFQINBOX_MODEL`.
- **Dev run:** 24 emails, 24 calls, 66,139 input / 19,913 output tokens, **$0.29**
  (about 1.2 cents per email; median 0.9 cents; the dearest are a 44-line PDF and a two-page
  phone scan at about 3.5 cents each). About 2 minutes, sequential.
- **Per email:** `cost_report.json` lists calls, tokens and dollars for every email;
  `calls`/`cost_usd` are what the answer cost when it was made, `new_calls`/`new_cost_usd` are
  what this run spent (zero on a replay). The totals are printed on stderr.
- **Expect** roughly $0.50 and 3–4 minutes for a 40-email inbox.
- Prices are a table in `rfqinbox/model.py` ($2.00 / $8.00 per million input / output tokens).

## Other commands

```
python -m rfqinbox inspect data/dev/emails/E005.eml     # what the model is shown for one email
python -m rfqinbox score parsed.json --gate             # exit 1 on any silent loss
```

## Tests (no key, no network)

```
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest
```

The tests remove `OPENAI_API_KEY` and switch `.env` loading off, so they can never spend money.

## The probe inbox

`eval/probes/` holds 17 invented emails (not dev) with their own key and cache; see
`eval/make_probes.py` and `eval/history.md`.

```
python -m rfqinbox parse --emails eval/probes/emails --out eval/probes/parsed.json --cache eval/probes/cache
python -m rfqinbox score eval/probes/parsed.json --key eval/probes/answer_key.json
```

# Decisions

Time spent: TODO (hours). One model call per email; everything checkable without judgment is code.

## Something in the data that surprised me

The biggest source of wrong output was an email the model read perfectly. A customer resent
an RFQ a day later with different wording and the same PDF. The model extracted all 44 lines
correctly, and every one of them was wrong, because the README says the later copy has no
lines. 44 of the first run's 45 hallucinated lines were that one email. Whether an answer is
right depended on a different email, so no prompt could fix it. That moved duplicates and
revision links out of the model entirely (`checks.link_records`).

## Something in the brief I disagree with, and what I did

`needs_review` is allowed only on requests. That leaves no honest answer for "I could not read
this and do not know what it is": calling it `other` risks a silent loss, the most expensive
failure. So anything unreadable or failed becomes `rfq` + `needs_review`. I accept the cost: if
the model is down, a vendor quote is reported as a request needing review (a phantom) rather
than dropped. I would rather the contract had an `unknown` class or allowed the flag everywhere.

Second, smaller: `raw` for a picture is "your reading of it", but lines are paired on `raw`
tokens. A nameplate has no single line, and the dev key uses only the model-number line. I
followed that (a code rule keeps the identifying line), but it is a guess from one example.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and the two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 210/210 lines and my own 17-email probe set is 39/39, but dev shaped the rules and I
wrote the probes, so I discount both.

| | prediction (~40 emails) |
|---|---|
| silent losses | 0 |
| hallucinated lines | 0–8 (one missed duplicate would be most of it) |
| lost / phantom requests | 0–1 / 0–1 |
| classification | 93–97% |
| line recall / precision | 94–98% / 93–98% |
| qty / uom / source | 96–99% / 97–100% / 97–100% |
| context carried | 90–96% |
| revises / duplicate links | 70–100% (few emails, so coarse) |
| needs_review precision / recall | 75–100% / 80–100% |

1. **Dense phone scans and photos.** The same scanned form gave 12 wrong quantities, then 0,
   then 1 across three runs. Sending pages in full-resolution bands fixed most of it, but
   small digits are still occasionally misread, and code cannot check a number that exists
   only in a picture.
2. **Threads and resends that do not look like dev's.** Duplicates need the same sender and
   either identical lines or provably identical content; a resend from a colleague's address,
   or a re-typed list, stays a normal request and all its lines count as hallucinated. A
   revision whose original is not quoted is rebuilt from whatever is in the email.

## How this runs for real

- **3,000 emails a day by webhook.** Each email is independent until linking, about 5 s and
  1.2 cents (roughly $36/day). *Built:* per-email isolation, atomic writes, a content-keyed
  cache, cost per email. *Not built:* the queue and workers; linking duplicates and revisions
  against a rolling window of earlier mail instead of one folder.
- **Provider down for two hours.** *Built:* timeouts, three retries with backoff on 429/5xx
  and network errors, then the email is flagged with the reason; failures are never cached,
  so the next run retries only those. *Not built:* a retry queue. In production I would park
  the email and alert, not emit a flagged record after 15 seconds.
- **A 300-page PDF.** *Built:* the reader stops at 40 text pages, 6 scanned pages and 60,000
  characters, says so in the text the model sees, and code flags the email for review with
  the lines it did read. *Not built:* splitting a long document across several calls.
- **The same email delivered twice.** *Built:* the second copy costs nothing (same cache key)
  and is marked `duplicate_of` the first. *Not built:* a lock. Two runs started at once both
  pay; I did this by accident and it cost $0.16.

## Where the model decides and where code decides

The model decides what kind of email it is, which text is a request, and what applies to each
line (headings, defaults and overrides, form fields, the rep's note on a forward). It writes
an `analysis` field first, kept in the cache and never in `parsed.json`.

Code decides everything that needs no judgment: what is quoted history, hidden or struck
through (the reader marks it before the model sees it); the output schema (one repair retry);
that every line's words appear in the email, else it is dropped and the email flagged; that
lines found only in hidden or struck content are dropped; `source` names; vague amounts and
sizes are not quantities; missing, unreadable, encrypted or truncated attachments are
flagged; duplicates and `revises`; and that a request with no lines is never left unflagged.

## How I measured

`rfqinbox score` implements the README's grading as I read it (the pairing threshold is my
guess); `eval/history.md` has a row per behaviour change. Dev alone could not tell me whether
I had fitted it, so I wrote `eval/probes/`: 17 invented emails. Their first run found two
real faults dev never showed (a partial override dropping the rest of a default; a nameplate
`raw`). Tests fail if the prompt contains any five-word run, name or part number from a dev
or probe email. That guard caught three dev phrases I had used as examples in prompt v1.

## Rejected, broken, next

- **Rejected:** the OpenAI SDK (one POST does not need it); local OCR (no wheels-only
  option); separate classify and extract calls (double the cost, no gain on dev); a
  rule-based classifier for when the model is down (a wrong confident answer is worse than
  a flag); fuzzy duplicate thresholds (a real one-line change would vanish).
- **Known broken or unverified:** not run on Windows; replay with no key depends on the
  reader producing the same text with the graders' library versions (unpinned); the tag rule
  relies on a list of field names; the price table is not checked against the live price list.
- **Next:** read scans twice and flag disagreements; pin versions; a queue; the matcher.

# AI usage

## Setup

- **Tool:** Claude Code (desktop app). TODO: confirm tool and model for the sessions before
  10:38 on 13 Nov (skeleton, scorer, reader, first CLAUDE.md).
- **Instruction file:** `CLAUDE.md` (in the repo): the task in one paragraph, hard rules
  (key never in the repo or logs, don't fit dev, flag when unsure), how we work (TDD, the
  human commits), layout, status, and what the dev data taught us.
- No subagents, skills or MCP servers were used for the work. `parse` uses the provided OpenAI
  key; the coding agent ran on my own account.

## How I worked

One chunk per pair of commits: the agent wrote failing tests and stopped; I read them and
committed "... (failing)"; then it wrote the code and I committed that. I ran every paid
`parse` myself and pasted the output back; the agent never handled the key. After each
behaviour change it replayed dev from the cache, scored it, and added a row to
`eval/history.md`. I reviewed by reading the tests (they state the behaviour), the score
diff, and the agent's list of judgment calls, and I pushed back on those: three of them were
revisited and one was changed. When the score looked too good I had it build a probe set of
invented emails to test on something that was not dev.

## Three moments

Session for all three: `ai-sessions/94cd2907-9e0a-412a-a5d5-a77d0da96bdb.jsonl`.

**The agent was wrong, and how I caught it.** Prompt v1 (`d63ae0f`) used three phrases
copied from dev emails as examples. The agent's own leak test passed because it only compared
the prompt with answer-key lines, senders and subjects. Before prompt v2 I reminded it of the
"don't fit dev" rule; it wrote stricter guards (`41c136e`: no five-word run, name or part
number from any dev email), which failed on v1, and v2 (`874c5ed`) removed the phrases.

**I overruled it.** The agent kept the rule "read the key from the environment only" and
gave me shell commands to load `.env`; they did not work from the app's command box and cost
several failed runs. I told it to load `.env` in code. It did (`e1bb609`), and added what I
had not asked for but needed: the real environment wins, and tests switch loading off so
`pytest` can never spend the key.

**It saved me real time.** One scanned form had 12 wrong quantities. Instead of rewording
the prompt, the agent rendered the page at the size the provider shrinks images to, showed
the digits were illegible there and clear at full size, and sent large pages as
full-resolution bands (`6c85c9d` tests, `b46e551` code). Quantity accuracy went from 94.3%
to 100% with one email re-read for 3.5 cents.
